label: The Boundary at Infinity
notes: Open by motivating the question. A complete CAT(0) space has no edge, yet we want to attach ideal points that record the directions in which geodesics escape. Stress that the entire construction rests on geodesic rays and a single equivalence: rays that stay a bounded distance apart name the same point at infinity.

label: Geodesic Rays
notes: Define a geodesic ray as an isometric embedding of the half-line. Emphasise that in a complete CAT(0) space rays exist in abundance: from any basepoint and any other point you can extend, and convexity of the metric keeps rays from oscillating. This is the raw material for every ideal point.

label: Asymptotic Rays
notes: Introduce the asymptotic relation. Two rays are asymptotic when the distance between corresponding points stays bounded for all time. Walk through why this is an equivalence relation, and note the picture: two rays leaving different basepoints but shadowing each other forever define one ideal direction.

label: The Visual Boundary
notes: Define the visual boundary as the set of asymptotic classes of rays. Give the key rigidity fact for complete CAT(0) spaces: from any basepoint exactly one ray represents each boundary point. So the boundary is canonically the set of rays issuing from a fixed origin, which we will topologise next.

label: The Cone Topology
notes: Explain the cone topology through nested neighbourhoods of a ray: fix a radius and a tolerance, and collect points and rays whose geodesics stay close out to that radius. Stress that the topology is independent of basepoint and that it glues the boundary smoothly onto the space, building the bar-X compactification.

label: Compactification
notes: State the compactness theorem: when X is proper and complete, bar-X is compact and the boundary is closed. The proof idea is Arzela-Ascoli on unit-speed rays from the basepoint. Warn that properness is essential; in infinite-dimensional CAT(0) spaces the visual boundary need not be compact.

label: Busemann Functions
notes: Define the Busemann function of a ray as the renormalised limit of distance functions. Each ray gives a 1-Lipschitz convex function whose level sets are horospheres. Highlight that adding a constant or choosing an asymptotic ray shifts the function by a constant, so it is well defined up to additive constant per boundary point.

label: Horoballs and Horospheres
notes: Describe sublevel sets of Busemann functions as horoballs, with horospheres as their boundaries. In Euclidean space horospheres are hyperplanes; in hyperbolic space they are the familiar tangent spheres. Convexity of the Busemann function makes every horoball convex, a fact used constantly when studying parabolic isometries.

label: Isometries Act on the Boundary
notes: Explain that every isometry of X extends to a homeomorphism of the boundary, because it sends rays to rays and preserves the asymptotic relation. This action classifies isometries: elliptic and hyperbolic ones have fixed structure inside X, while parabolics fix a boundary point and preserve its horoballs.

label: Example: Euclidean Space
notes: Work the cleanest example. The boundary of n-dimensional Euclidean space is the round sphere of directions, since two rays are asymptotic exactly when they are parallel and point the same way. Busemann functions are affine, horospheres are hyperplanes. This is the model every other example is compared against.

label: Examples: Trees and Hyperbolic Space
notes: Contrast two further boundaries. A simplicial tree has a totally disconnected Cantor-set boundary of ends, reflecting branching. Hyperbolic n-space again has a sphere boundary, but the cone topology now carries the conformal structure visible at infinity. Together these show how curvature shapes the boundary.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tying the three viewpoints together: rays give points, the cone topology compactifies, Busemann functions give horofunctions. Remind students that the boundary is a quasi-isometry-flavoured invariant in the hyperbolic setting but only a CAT(0)-isometry invariant in general, and preview its use in rigidity and group actions.
